ov: A quiet novella narrated by an unnamed daughter who takes her mother on a trip to Japan. Nothing dramatic happens. The story lives in what is not said: the mother’s migration from Hong Kong, the language they do not share, and the gaps in what a daughter can ever know about her parent. In the Common Module, it asks how strength and vulnerability sit side by side, and what endurance looks like when it is silent.
rub: Language, forms and features: first-person restraint, understatement, repeated questions and the motif of photography shape what we feel.
Identity, culture and acceptance: the narrator and her mother belong to Hong Kong, Australia and neither fully.
Agency and conformity: both women hold back; the narrator acts (she plans the trip) yet withdraws when closeness is offered.
sum: An adult daughter and her mother travel through Japan in autumn, during typhoon season. The daughter planned the trip in the hope of reaching her mother. She watches the mother carefully: her tidy clothes, her small purchases, her patient silences. As they move between trains, museums, tea houses, a bathhouse and a mountain of shrine gates, the narrator drifts into memories of her family, a sister, an uncle who has died, her own relationships, and the stories her mother has never told. She imagines her mother’s early years as a migrant, but admits she can only guess. By the end of the trip the daughter feels it has not done what she wanted. A final image of the two women, tired and alike in a photograph, and the daughter kneeling to help her mother with a shoe, offers a quiet, unresolved closeness.
acts: Rain, a crowded station and a museum visit. The narrator introduces her mother (careful dress, the same suitcase of her childhood) and explains why she chose Japan: to be on “equal footing” as strangers.
The narrator takes a photo and her mother assumes a stiff pose. Memories surface of family history, the mother’s photographs and television shows from Hong Kong.
The narrator tries to picture her mother’s first months in Australia and what she gave up. The questions stay unanswered.
She reflects on her mother’s Cantonese and her own English, and on how rarely the two women speak in the language that would bring them close.
Sun at last. At a hillside of small shrine gates the mother buys gifts for others and the narrator takes a picture of them together, hand in hand.
At a shop in a converted temple the mother waits, still as a statue. She asks for help with her shoe, and the narrator kneels to give it.
ch: Observant and reserved. She plans the trip to bridge a gap with her mother, yet repeatedly hesitates to speak or ask. Her narration is a way of getting close without risking rejection.
I tried, and failed, to imagine her first months there.
Dignified, private and watchful. She dresses with care, gives gifts and rarely speaks of the past. She is known to the reader only through the daughter’s guesses.
Is this all right, she asked me, or should I stand over there, nearer to that tree?
Mentioned in memory and in gifts for her children. She represents the family left at home and a different way of growing up.
(The mother) had bought two sets of brightly colored gloves for my sister’s children.
A figure of family grief the mother has not fully discussed. He stands for the untold stories that haunt the novella.
My mother’s stories—whatever she had, or had not told us about my uncle, or her early days in a new country.
cx: Jessica Au is a Melbourne-based writer. Cold Enough for Snow won the inaugural Novel Prize run by Giramondo (Australia), New Directions (US) and Fitzcarraldo Editions (UK), and has been translated into many languages. It is fiction, not memoir, but draws on the experience of a daughter of migrants. Check your class notes for how your teacher frames the author’s background.

Diaspora, second-generation experience and the gap between a parent’s language and a child’s. Cantonese is the mother’s first language; English is the narrator’s. The novella shows how a culture can be carried in food, clothing and gifts even when it is not spoken about.

Hong Kong was a British colony until 1997, which is why the narrator remarks on her mother’s “near-perfect, colonial English”. The mother’s migration to Australia and the many small adjustments of the first months are part of Australia’s multicultural history.

Intergenerational silence: children of migrants often know little of what their parents endured. Travel as a way of trying to repair family distance. Photography and art as ways of looking at a person without speaking to them.
im: Photographs are the central image. The mother’s “stock pose” (feet together, back straight, hands clasped) contrasts with the daughter’s wish to catch her “during ordinary time”. The final photograph of them together shows them “weary, surprised and somehow very alike”.
Museum and art: the narrator looks at paintings and ceramics and describes what she sees in flat, careful sentences, as if looking can substitute for speaking.
Snow: the mother’s only stated wish is to know whether winter there is “cold enough for snow”. Snow becomes a symbol of the experiences she has never had.
Rain, trains and crowds: the opening rain and the crowd “like a current” keep the two women close and slightly adrift.
th: The trip is meant to close a gap between mother and daughter, but silence and politeness keep them apart.
Common Module: the paradoxes of motivation and behaviour.
Identity is formed by place and heritage, but also by what is withheld. The narrator feels “at home in a place that was not mine”.
Common Module: identity, culture, acceptance and growth.
Different first languages create intimacy and distance. What goes unsaid is as meaningful as what is said.
Common Module: the power of language to express personal ideas and experiences.
The narrator reconstructs her mother’s past from guesses, objects and questions.
Common Module: lived experience seen through the narrator’s perspective.
The mother’s quiet endurance and gift-giving are forms of strength; the narrator’s hesitation exposes her vulnerability.
Common Module Q1: assumptions about strength and vulnerability.

A.i: Jessica Au’s Cold Enough for Snow effectively offers audiences insight into cultural and intellectual opportunities that challenge assumptions about strength and vulnerability, through the tension between conformity and agency. Through the narrator’s journey in Japan with her mother, Au explores how unfamiliar cultural environments can expose vulnerability while also encouraging growth and independence. Her restrained first-person voice invites audiences to reconsider whether strength lies in certainty, or in a willingness to remain open to what cannot be known.
b: Au suggests that vulnerability is not the opposite of strength but a condition of it. The narrator reflects, “It was strange at once to be so familiar and yet so separated. I wondered how I could feel so at home in a place that was not mine.” The paradox of feeling both familiar and separated highlights her complex sense of belonging, suggesting that identity is shaped by personal experience, not simply cultural background. This challenges the assumption that individuals must conform to a particular culture to feel accepted. Similarly, Au writes that she hoped the trip would “put us on equal footing in some way, to both be made strangers.” The paradox of becoming strangers to achieve equality reveals that shared vulnerability can create connection across cultural difference. Human strength therefore emerges through accepting uncertainty rather than relying on familiarity.

Furthermore, Au exposes the limits of agency within the mother–daughter relationship. When the narrator photographs her mother, “she assumed a stock pose: feet together, back straight, hands clasped.” The list of rigid positions shows the mother conforming to how she believes she should be seen, concealing the inner self the narrator wants to capture. When the mother then offers to photograph her, the narrator replies, “I said no, that we had better move on.” The juxtaposition between the mother’s invitation and the daughter’s refusal exposes the narrator’s hesitation and difficulty exercising agency, withholding the reciprocity that might make both women visible. Strength, in Au’s world, is complicated by fear of being known.

Finally, Au shows that strength is found in small acts of care. The mother buys gifts, and the narrator realises that “everything she had bought here was a gift for someone else.” The plain declarative shifts our assumptions about strength from self-assertion to selflessness. In the closing image, the narrator concedes that in the photograph they were “weary, surprised and somehow very alike”, and the triplet gathers two women into one picture. The final gesture of kneeling to help her mother with a shoe reverses the earlier refusal, suggesting that connection can emerge through quiet vulnerability.
A.c: Ultimately, Au challenges audiences to reconsider the relationship between strength and vulnerability, demonstrating that personal growth can emerge through the uncertainty of navigating cultural identity and resisting expectations. By the end of the novella, strength is no longer certainty but the willingness to kneel, to ask for help, and to be seen.
A.n: What to notice: a thesis that answers both words in the question (strength AND vulnerability). Each paragraph opens with an idea, not a retelling. Quotes are short and woven into sentences. Each technique (paradox, list, juxtaposition, triplet) is named and its effect explained. Module language (assumptions, agency and conformity) keeps returning.

B.i: In Cold Enough for Snow, Jessica Au shows how human strength and vulnerability can exist together. Through the narrator’s trip to Japan with her mother, she explores culture, identity and family relationships.
b: Au shows vulnerability through the narrator’s feelings of belonging. She says, “It was strange at once to be so familiar and yet so separated.” This paradox shows that she feels at home but also like an outsider. It shows that identity is not just about where you come from. Au also says they would be “on equal footing” as “strangers”, which shows that being vulnerable together can help people connect.

Au also shows the difficulty of connection. When the narrator takes a photo, her mother “assumed a stock pose.” This shows she is trying to look the way she thinks she should. Later, the mother offers to take a photo and the narrator says no. This shows that the narrator is nervous and does not know how to be close to her mother.

At the end, the narrator and her mother look “weary, surprised and somehow very alike” in a photo. This shows that they have a connection. The narrator kneels to help her mother with her shoe, which shows love and care.
B.c: In conclusion, Au shows that strength and vulnerability go together. The narrator and her mother grow closer through their trip and Au challenges assumptions about culture and identity.
B.n: What to notice: a clear argument and well-chosen quotes, but the effect is more general (“this shows…”). Techniques are named less precisely, and the analysis does not always tie back to “assumptions” in the question. The conclusion repeats instead of synthesising.

models.C: In Cold Enough for Snow the narrator goes to Japan with her mother. The narrator takes a photo of her mother and she does a pose. This shows that the mother is vulnerable. The author uses description. It is about strength and vulnerability.

A.i: Jessica Au’s Cold Enough for Snow enriches our understanding of the endurance of the human spirit by representing a particular life, a migrant mother’s, through what remains unsaid. Au suggests that endurance is not heroic triumph but quiet, cumulative adaptation. Told through her daughter’s limited, searching perspective, the mother’s life is revealed in small gestures, absences and guesses, inviting audiences to value the unrecorded resilience of those who leave one home for another.
b: Au represents endurance as the weight of countless small adjustments. Imagining her mother’s arrival in Australia, the narrator admits, “I tried, and failed, to imagine her first months there.” The anaphora of “Had she been homesick? Had she been awed…? Had she been worn out…” builds a chain of unanswerable questions, and positions the audience to feel the distance between generations. The list that follows, “the supermarkets that were so well stocked, but where you could not buy glass noodles”, reveals that migration is endured through daily losses, not dramatic events. The “bank teller unable to understand her near-perfect, colonial English” adds irony, as mastery of language cannot guarantee being understood. The mother’s life is thus enriched, for readers, by seeing endurance in the ordinary.

Au also presents endurance as habit and silence. The narrator speculates that her mother “had found the past harder and harder to evoke, especially with no one to remember it with,” and that this had become “another thing she grew used to, like eating cereal for breakfast, or keeping your shoes on in other people’s homes, or rarely speaking to another in your mother tongue.” The accumulating list equates profound loss with trivial routine, suggesting that survival requires forgetting as well as remembering. The loss of the mother tongue becomes the most painful adaptation, as the narrator and her mother “only ever spoke together in one, and not the other.” Endurance, then, is shown as costly.

Finally, Au suggests that the spirit endures through care and unfulfilled desire. The mother’s only question about Japan is whether it is “cold enough for snow, which she had never seen”, and the title makes this longing a symbol of experiences postponed. The narrator realises that “everything she had bought here was a gift for someone else”, a plain declarative that reveals a life organised around others. The closing photograph shows the two as “weary, surprised and somehow very alike”, offering a moment of recognition across the distance. Through the mother’s particular life, we understand endurance as generosity and wanting, not only survival.
A.c: Au’s representation of one mother’s life therefore deepens our understanding of the human spirit’s endurance as quiet, costly and unfinished. By showing what the daughter cannot know, she asks audiences to honour the lives that endure without telling their story.
A.n: What to notice: the thesis defines “endurance” in a fresh way (quiet, cumulative) and every paragraph proves it. Quotes are short; techniques (anaphora, list, irony, symbol) are named and their effect on the audience is explained. “Particular life” is kept in view, and each paragraph ends by linking back to “enriches our understanding”.

B.i: In Cold Enough for Snow, Jessica Au shows the endurance of the human spirit through the life of the narrator’s mother. The mother has moved from Hong Kong to Australia and has dealt with many challenges.
b: Au shows the mother’s endurance through the narrator’s questions. She says, “I tried, and failed, to imagine her first months there.” She asks, “Had she been homesick? Had she been awed by the streets?” This shows that she doesn’t know what her mother went through. The list of small things, like the supermarkets and the bank teller, shows that migrants have many struggles.

Au also shows endurance through the mother’s silence. The narrator says her mother may have found the past “harder and harder to evoke” and that it became “another thing she grew used to.” This shows that the mother has coped by not talking about the past. The narrator also says that she and her mother speak in only one language, which shows they have distance.

The mother is also shown to be caring. The narrator realises that “everything she had bought here was a gift for someone else.” Her question about snow shows she has wishes of her own. This shows that the mother’s spirit is strong.
B.c: In conclusion, Au shows the endurance of the human spirit through the mother’s life. The mother is strong because she has survived migration and still cares for her family.
B.n: What to notice: relevant quotes and a clear point, but the paragraphs describe (“this shows that…”) rather than evaluate. Techniques are only occasionally named (list), the effect on the reader is not explained, and “enriches our understanding” is not addressed directly.

fc: What is anaphora and where does Au use it?
Repetition at the start of clauses. Au uses it in “Had she been homesick? Had she been awed…? Had she been worn out…” to build unanswerable questions about the mother’s migration.
What does the mother’s “stock pose” suggest?
She performs how she believes she should be seen: a quiet conformity that conceals her inner self.
Which quote shows the paradox of belonging?
“It was strange at once to be so familiar and yet so separated.”
What does “cold enough for snow” symbolise?
The mother’s quiet longing and the experiences she has never had. It is her only stated wish for the trip.
How does the ending reverse the earlier photograph scene?
Earlier the narrator refuses to be photographed (“we had better move on”). At the end she kneels to help her mother with a shoe, offering care and closeness.
